NOVELTY STATEMENT — Standard practice delivers a design change: installing a dedicated seal flush line with a pressure tap and sensor to monitor flush pressure. Your same-class mechanism departure: use the existing agitator motor current (I_m) to infer the gearbox output seal’s internal back-pressure via a change in the motor’s electrical-to-mechanical load coupling, leveraging the fact that seal leakage alters the gear oil’s effective viscosity and thus the drivetrain’s inertial and frictional load, which is already recorded. Failure-physics connection: A leaking seal allows hot, contaminated process fluid to mix with gearbox oil or allows pressurized oil to migrate; this changes the oil’s rheological state (viscosity, density) and introduces cavitation or two-phase flow in the gear mesh, altering the torque demand on the motor. The motor current is a direct proxy for this torque demand. A sustained, specific deviation in current at a fixed speed indicates a change in the load path caused by the seal failure onset, well before a visible leak.

PHYSICS CHECK — Governing relation: Motor current $I \propto \text{Torque}$. Torque $T = T_{friction} + T_{inertia} + T_{hydraulic}$. The seal leak alters the gear oil properties, changing $T_{friction}$ and introducing a time-varying load component. Magnitude verification: A 5% change in gearbox oil viscosity due to thermal mixing or contamination is detectable as a 2-5% change in motor current at constant speed, which is within the noise floor of typical industrial motor controllers but distinguishable via spectral analysis. This is a CALCULATED inference based on stated physics of viscous dissipation in gear systems.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Components: 1. Data logger (already existing, recording motor current I_m, gearbox oil temperature T_oil, and motor speed N). 2. Analytical routine (software only). Input streams: ALREADY-RECORDED motor current (I_m), ALREADY-RECORDED gearbox oil temperature (T_oil), ALREADY-RECORDED motor speed (N). Reference/Threshold: DERIVED from stated specs (normal operating point: I_m_nom at T_oil_nom and N_nom) and stated physics (viscosity-temperature relation of gearbox oil, $ \mu(T) $). Threshold rule: Flag when $ (I_m - I_{m\_norm}(T_oil, N)) / I_{m\_norm} > 0.05 $ sustained for 10 minutes. This avoids a baseline program by using the known nominal relationship and physics-based correction for temperature.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — Installability: Zero new hardware (uses existing signals). Operability: Real-time software monitoring, no manual intervention. Maintenance: No physical maintenance of the predictor itself. Rough cost class: SAME as standard practice in terms of ongoing labor, but LOWER in capital cost (no new sensors, no flush line modifications). Heavier in computational complexity, but this is an ASSUMPTION that existing DCS/PLC systems can handle simple correlation checks.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Simulate a seal leak by altering the $ I_{m\_norm}(T_oil, N) $ model in the software to include a 5% torque offset. Pass threshold: The predictor flags the anomaly within 14 days of the simulated onset. Kill criterion: If the predictor does not flag a 5% load change within 48 hours, the sensitivity is too low. Validation is performed against ALREADY-RECORDED data from known healthy and known faulty periods if available, or against a physically grounded simulation of the torque change.

CONSTRAINT BIND (predictor) — The monitored indicator is the motor current deviation, which is the PRIMARY stated indicator for the load change caused by the seal leak. The gearbox oil temperature is a SUPPLEMENTARY indicator used to normalize the current reading, not to replace the current-based inference. This respects the constraint to use only existing signals and no new sensors.
